title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 28: Manila International Airport Authority v. City of Parañaque: The Power of Local Governments to Tax National Government Instrumentalities
keywords: Manila International Airport Authority v. City of Parañaque
Mactan-Cebu International Airport Authority v. Marcos
Office of the Government Corporate Counsel
primary_topics: Chapter 28 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Manila International Airport Authority v. City of Parañaque, in which the Court, through Justice Antonio T. Carpio, held the real properties of MIAA exempt from the real estate tax imposed by a local government and voided the assessments and the auction sale.

The two pillars of the majority ruling: MIAA is not a government-owned or -controlled corporation but an instrumentality of the national government covered by Section 133(o) of the Local Government Code, and its airport land and buildings are owned by the Republic and therefore exempt under Section 234(a).

The property-law consequence: airport land and buildings are properties of public dominion under Article 420 of the Civil Code, outside human commerce, not subject to levy or auction sale, with MIAA holding title merely in trust for the Republic.

The Dissent of Justice Dante O. Tinga, joined by Justices Martinez and Callejo, arguing that Mactan-Cebu International Airport Authority v. Marcos and a dozen precedents were overturned without explanation, that MIAA is a GOCC performing proprietary functions and liable for realty taxes, but that its charter still bars the sale or disposition of its properties, leaving the city only a limited lien.
sub_topics: Under Executive Order 903, the Revised Charter of the MIAA, petitioner was created to administer and operate the NAIA Complex in Parañaque City, and some 600 hectares of land including the runways and buildings were transferred to it from the Bureau of Air Transportation.

In 1997 the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel opined that the Local Government Code had withdrawn MIAA's exemption under Section 21 of EO 903, so MIAA negotiated and paid part of the tax; it then received Final Notices of Real Estate Tax Delinquency totalling P624,506,725.42 for 1992 to 2001, followed by notices and warrants of levy.
On August 9, 2001 the OGCC reversed itself, opining that Section 21 of the MIAA Charter together with Section 206 of the Local Government Code exempted petitioner from real estate tax.

MIAA's Petition for prohibition and injunction was dismissed by the Court of Appeals for having been filed out of time, while the city published and posted notices of a public auction sale set for February 7, 2003 -- on which day the Court issued an immediately effective temporary restraining order.
After Oral Argument on March 29, 2005, the threshold issue was whether the airport land and buildings were exempt from real estate tax under existing laws.

The Court held first that MIAA was not a GOCC: under the Administrative Code a GOCC must be organized as a stock or non-stock corporation, but MIAA had no capital stock divided into shares, no stockholders or voting shares, and no members, and was mandated to remit 20 percent of its annual gross operating income to the national treasury.

Nor was it organized for any of the charitable, religious, educational or similar purposes that Section 88 of the Corporation Code assigns to nonstock corporations; being a public utility, it was organized to operate the Manila airports for public use.

MIAA was instead a government instrumentality vested with corporate powers, able to exercise eminent domain, police authority and the levying of fees and charges, and thus fell under Section 133(o) of the Local Government Code, which bars local taxes, fees or charges of any kind on the National Government, its agencies and instrumentalities.

The Court restated the canons of taxation at work: a tax is never presumed, the law imposing it must be expressed in clear language, doubt about taxability is resolved against taxation, exemptions are strictly construed against the taxpayer but an exemption granted by Congress to a national government instrumentality is construed liberally in its favor.

There was no reason for local governments to tax national instrumentalities rendering essential public services, the only exception being where the legislature clearly intended it for sound and compelling policy considerations, in language that must be explicit.

The airport land and buildings were properties of public dominion under Article 420 of the Civil Code, the term 'ports' covering airports as well as seaports, and they were devoted to public use for international and domestic travel; collecting terminal fees did not remove that character, such fees being a user's tax that is more equitable because paid only by those who actually use the facility.

Being outside human commerce, such properties could not be levied upon, encumbered or auctioned, and any such levy or sale was void as contrary to public policy, so the city could not compel the auction of the 600-hectare runway.
Before MIAA could encumber the land the President first had to withdraw it from public use under the Public Land Law, Commonwealth Act No. 141, a prerequisite respondents failed to show had been met.

MIAA held title merely in trust for the Republic; its executive head could not even sign a deed of conveyance, and the transfer from the Bureau of Air Transportation was meant only to reorganize a division into an autonomous body, leaving the Republic the beneficial owner of the properties and the sole owner of MIAA.

Section 234(a) exempts real property owned by the Republic unless its beneficial use has been granted to a taxable person; since MIAA was not a taxable person under Section 133(o), the exemption held -- but portions leased to private entities were taxable, the beneficial use there having been granted for consideration to taxable persons.
The Court accordingly declared the MIAA properties exempt and voided the assessments, the Final Notices of Delinquency (except as to the leased portions) and the auction sale and all its effects.

Justice Tinga's Dissent accused the majority of veering wildly off-course and shattering statutes and precedents to protect the precious Ming vase that is the MIAA, overturning at least one dozen precedents, and faulted it for not explaining why Mactan -- involving a similarly situated airport authority -- was wrong.

For the Dissent, the legislative charter governs the definition of a corporation created by Congress, so MIAA, whose charter lets it acquire property, incur obligations, sue and be sued, and bear a corporate name, seal and bylaws, is a GOCC notwithstanding the Corporation or Administrative Code.

The Dissent read Section 193 of the Local Government Code as withdrawing all tax exemptions of all persons including GOCCs, rendering Section 21 of EO 903 ineffectual, and Sections 3 and 22 of the MIAA charter as explicitly transferring ownership of the airport land and buildings to MIAA with no trust provision.

It argued that under Section 234(a) it is the identity of the beneficial user, not the beneficial owner, that matters; that 'the Republic' is illuminated by the phrase 'political subdivisions', which the Constitution defines as provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays exercising sovereign functions; and that MIAA performs proprietary functions, airport operation being neither indispensable nor obligatory for the national government.

Justice Tinga nevertheless agreed that Section 3 of the MIAA charter bars the sale or disposition of its properties without presidential approval, a prohibition the Local Government Code did not withdraw, so the city was barred from seizing or auctioning them and was left with only a limited lien.

notable_anecdotes: The government's own lawyers changed sides mid-dispute: the OGCC first opined in 1997 that MIAA's exemption had been withdrawn, prompting it to pay part of the tax, then clarified on August 9, 2001 that it was exempt after all.

The city came within a day of selling the country's principal airport: notices of a February 7, 2003 auction were published in the Inquirer and posted around Parañaque, and only an immediately effective temporary restraining order issued on the day itself stopped the sale.
The delinquency claimed for 1992 to 2001 came to P624,506,725.42, and the property at stake included a 600-hectare complex with the runways themselves.

Justice Tinga opened his Dissent with an image that became the case's best-known line, accusing the majority of shattering statutes and judicial precedents left and right to protect the precious Ming vase that is the Manila International Airport Authority.

The Court noted a small point of tax philosophy along the way: terminal fees are a user's tax, collected only from those who actually use the facility rather than from everyone, and therefore more equitable.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 28 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Manila International Airport Authority v. City of Parañaque, in which the Court through Justice Antonio T. Carpio held the real properties of MIAA exempt from local real estate tax. Created under Executive Order 903 to operate the NAIA Complex, MIAA had received from the city Final Notices of Real Estate Tax Delinquency totalling P624,506,725.42 for 1992 to 2001 and then warrants of levy, after the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel first opined that the Local Government Code had withdrawn its exemption and later reversed itself; the Court of Appeals dismissed its Petition as filed out of time, and only a temporary restraining order issued on February 7, 2003 stopped the scheduled auction of the airport. Following Oral Argument, the Court held that MIAA was not a government-owned or -controlled corporation, having no capital stock divided into shares, no stockholders and no members, and not being organized for any purpose the Corporation Code assigns to nonstock corporations, but a government instrumentality vested with corporate powers and therefore covered by Section 133(o), which bars local taxes on the National Government, its agencies and instrumentalities. A tax is never presumed, the Court said; doubt about taxability is resolved against taxation, and an exemption granted by Congress to a national instrumentality is construed liberally in its favor. It further held that the airport land and buildings were properties of public dominion under Article 420 of the Civil Code, devoted to public use, outside human commerce and therefore beyond levy or auction sale, with MIAA holding title merely in trust for the Republic and the President alone able to withdraw them from public use. Since MIAA was not a taxable person, Section 234(a) exempted the Republic's property, except for portions leased to private entities, whose beneficial use had been granted for consideration. The assessments, notices and auction sale were declared void. Justice Tinga, joined by Justices Martinez and Callejo, dissented, accusing the majority of overturning Mactan and a dozen precedents to protect 'the precious Ming vase that is the Manila International Airport Authority', arguing that MIAA is a GOCC performing proprietary functions and taxable, but agreeing that its charter bars any sale of its properties, leaving the city only a limited lien.
